content.text: Northeastern entrepreneurs turn ideas into real-world innovations

Ke Zhang, a professor of chemistry and chemical biology, and his spinout company PacDNA, Inc. are at the forefront of drug delivery to improve gene regulation. The revolutionary work could someday transform medicine and address rare diseases like muscular dystrophy.

Jenna Woods studied the mineral olivine on co-op as an undergrad. She discovered that when the rock reacts with atmospheric CO2 and water, it undergoes a chemical process that removes carbon from the air.

Woods now heads AngelRock BV, a company that aims to make olivine part of the global climate change solution.

In 2020, Northeastern alum Vicente Zavarce launched Yummy, Venezuela’s only delivery app. Working in the Bay Area during his co-op ignited Zavarce’s passion for entrepreneurship. His company is now valued at $200 million.

content.text:
Next Up Founders Prize
Application Guide
You will then be emailed a consent form, which must be completed before the application is sent to you. If you are under 18, a parent or guardian must complete the consent form on your behalf.

We recommend you draft your written responses ahead of time so you can revise them and check your word counts before submitting. You can also save your progress and return to finish your application later.
Give yourself time to plan and record your video pitch, since it should reflect the same problem, idea, and customer story you describe in your written answers.
Each applicant completes their own individual submission, even if you are applying as part of a team.
If you are applying with a team:
Every teammate must submit their own entry and list the same team name and team members so your submissions can be linked together.
Check in with your teammates before you start so that everyone submits the same answers to the venture and project questions, since we will review your team’s submissions together.
Your name, grade level, school name, school city, school state or region, school country, and preferred contact email and phone number
Whether you are applying as an individual or with a team, and if applying with a team, your team name and teammates’ names
A guidance counselor, teacher, or academic contact name and email
A note on word counts: Each of the written questions below has a 150-word limit. If you answer “Yes” to accelerator or program participation, that response has its own separate 100-word limit.
The problem: What problem is your venture or project solving, and for whom?
The idea: Describe your venture or project or concept. What are you building?
The AI angle: How does AI feature in your idea, as the product, the way you built it, or how you’ll reach customers?
The customer: Who would use or buy your idea, and what have you done to show they want or need it? Tell us what you tested and what you learned.
Why you: Why do you or your team care about this problem? What makes you positioned to build it, and why will you or your team succeed?
Your stage: Is your venture idea-stage (concept only), already operating (built and in use), or already scaled (established revenue and growth)?

Funding received: Has your venture or project received any outside funding, from a pitch competition, grant, crowdfunding, family or friends, or an investor? If you select any “Yes” option, you will also be asked who provided the funding, such as family or friends, a school or educational organization, a pitch or business plan competition, a grant or fellowship, crowdfunding, or an angel investor or venture capital firm.

Accelerator or program participation: Have you or anyone on your team participated in an entrepreneurship accelerator, incubator, or similar program related to this venture or idea? If you select “Yes,” you will also be asked to name the program(s) and briefly describe the involvement.
Social media presence: Does your venture or project have a social media presence? If you select “Yes,” you will also be asked to share the link(s), such as Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, or a website.
Video Submission: Upload your 2 to 3 minute video pitch (MP4, MOV, or similar format).
Growth: If you or your team is selected, what would you do with the recognition, mentorship, and prize?
Finals participation: If you advance to the Finals, would you be interested in pitching in person at Northeastern University’s Boston campus* during Global Entrepreneurship Week?

Questions? Contact Rachel Schrottman at r.schrottman@northeastern.edu.

——–

Your submission will be used solely for the evaluation of your application. All materials will remain confidential to our judging panel. By uploading your video and submitting your written responses, you grant Northeastern University a non-exclusive, non-commercial license to use these materials for educational and promotional purposes. You keep all rights to your underlying idea. Full details are in the Official Rules.

*Travel costs are not covered and would be at your own expense. Finalists attending high school outside the United States must participate by video unless they have independent legal means of entering the U.S. A video submission carries equal weight in judging, whether or not you plan to attend in person.

content.text: Applications for the 2026 Next Up Founders Prize are now closed. Thank you to everyone who applied!

In the Next Up Founders Prize competition, you’ll pitch to founders and innovators and get feedback to advance your ideas—and winners walk away with a piece of $100k+ in cash prizes to fund your idea. You’ll join a community that keeps supporting you after the competition, earn an official LinkedIn badge, and gain access to Northeastern’s global entrepreneurship network—with 2,600+ ventures supported and 8,000+ mentorship matches connecting founders and investors worldwide.

Whether your interests lie in engineering, health sciences, psychology, design, education, or computer science, show us how you’re pushing the boundaries of innovation and where AI fits into your build—whether that’s in the product itself, how you built it, or how you plan to launch it.

content.text:
If you’re a high school student building
something, you’re eligible.
No connection to Northeastern is required to enter—this competition is open to any high school founder, anywhere.
Any high school student over 13 years of age, grades 9–12.
Enter solo or with up to three teammates, for a maximum of four. Each team member must submit their own individual entry. No student may be part of more than one team.
Any stage counts—a concept, a working prototype, or an early operating venture.
Public, private, charter, or home-schooled students all qualify.
Open globally in any field. This isn’t limited to Northeastern applicants.
A teacher, counselor, or mentor can serve as your school contact.
Share your name, date of birth, country, and parent/guardian contact information so we can confirm you’re eligible to enter.
Every entrant must sign a consent form agreeing to the Contest rules. If you’re under 18, this form is sent to your parent or guardian to sign on your behalf.

Once your eligibility is confirmed and your consent form is complete, we’ll email you the full Application — including your school and contact details, and a written description of the problem you’re solving, your idea, and your AI angle.
Upload a video pitching your idea, along with your written answers, as part of your Application.
Advance to the semifinals, then pitch in Boston

A Reading Committee reviews all Applications in the virtual semifinal round. If you’re selected as a finalist, you’ll pitch in person on our Boston campus during Global Entrepreneurship Week, or you may choose to pitch via video.
Mid-October, depending on Reading Committee’s availability
Final pitch and Global Entrepreneurship Week Celebration
Between November 17 and 20, additional details to follow

Applications closed on September 30. All completed Applications will be reviewed by our Reading Committee during the semifinal round in October. Finalists will be notified in November and compete for prizes during Global Entrepreneurship Week, either in person in Boston or via video.
What’s the date, time, and location of the finale?
The finale will take place on our Boston campus in November. Finalists may opt to pitch virtually.
How will I know if I’m a finalist?
Finalists will be notified directly. All applicants will be notified of their status by email.
Students will be evaluated across four key areas: Innovation and originality, use of artificial intelligence, market potential and feasibility, and communication and pitch quality.

Your applications and pitches are reviewed by a panel that includes Northeastern staff and leading entrepreneurs from around the world — founders and investors who’ve built ventures and will give you meaningful feedback.
Up to $100K in cash prizes across finalists.
Can I appeal the judges’ decision?
All decisions of the judging panel are final.

events.title: Technology & Entrepreneurship for Good! featuring Catalin Voss, Founder of Ello

featured_media.note: event image is a PDF flyer (with QR code); first page rasterised

events.rest_excerpt_html: Catalin Voss is a German-Romanian inventor and social entrepreneur who first came to the United States at the age of 15 to build iPhone applications for a venture-backed startup before enrolling at Stanford University. While a student at Stanford, Voss created the Autism Glass Project, which developed emotion-recognition software to assist autistic children with recognizing social cues exchanged with other people. Winner of MIT’s Lemelson Award, Voss has built and sold several startups focused on building practical applications of AI for social impact. He has used machine learning to identify disparities in Parole Hearing transcripts, brought (and won) a legal case against the the State of California, built a low cost point-of-sale system for small shops in East Africa (acquired by Mastercard), and developed computer vision algorithms to identify methane-seeping holes in the arctic ice. His latest endeavor is Y-Combinator startup Ello, building an AI Teacher Reading Coach.
